# CLI reference

This page is generated from the Cobra command tree returned by `newRootCommand` in [`cmd/khora`](../../cmd/khora). Regenerate it with:

```sh
./scripts/generate-docs.sh
```

Check it for staleness with `./scripts/check-generated.sh`.

## `khora`

khora is the CLI for the sandbox engine.

It wraps the control-plane REST and Connect-RPC APIs, providing commands for sandbox lifecycle,
file operations, volumes, templates, network configuration, and event streaming.

```text
khora [flags]
```

| Option | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--api` | `http://127.0.0.1:8080` | API base URL |
| `--ca-cert` | `""` | PEM CA bundle used to verify the API server |
| `--client-cert` | `""` | PEM client certificate for mTLS |
| `--client-key` | `""` | PEM private key for the mTLS client certificate |
| `-v, --version` | `false` | version for khora |

## `khora completion`

Generate the autocompletion script for khora for the specified shell.
See each sub-command's help for details on how to use the generated script.

```text
khora completion
```

## `khora completion bash`

Generate the autocompletion script for the bash shell.

This script depends on the 'bash-completion' package.
If it is not installed already, you can install it via your OS's package manager.

To load completions in your current shell session:

	source <(khora completion bash)

To load completions for every new session, execute once:

#### Linux:

	khora completion bash > /etc/bash_completion.d/khora

#### macOS:

	khora completion bash > $(brew --prefix)/etc/bash_completion.d/khora

You will need to start a new shell for this setup to take effect.

```text
khora completion bash
```

| Option | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--no-descriptions` | `false` | disable completion descriptions |

## `khora completion zsh`

Generate the autocompletion script for the zsh shell.

If shell completion is not already enabled in your environment you will need
to enable it.  You can execute the following once:

	echo "autoload -U compinit; compinit" >> ~/.zshrc

To load completions in your current shell session:

	source <(khora completion zsh)

To load completions for every new session, execute once:

#### Linux:

	khora completion zsh > "${fpath[1]}/_khora"

#### macOS:

	khora completion zsh > $(brew --prefix)/share/zsh/site-functions/_khora

You will need to start a new shell for this setup to take effect.

```text
khora completion zsh [flags]
```

| Option | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--no-descriptions` | `false` | disable completion descriptions |

## `khora events`

Stream lifecycle events

```text
khora events
```

## `khora events follow`

Follow lifecycle events.

Replay is by cursor, and delivery is at-least-once: an event can be reported twice, so
anything consuming this programmatically should dedup on the event ID rather than trust
the sequence alone.

--wait hands the waiting to the engine, which returns the moment an event lands. That is
why --interval is not the detection latency: it is only reached after a wait expires with
nothing new.

```text
khora events follow [flags]
```

Aliases: `tail`, `watch`

| Option | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--after` | `0` | sequence number to start after |
| `--interval` | `1s` | poll interval when caught up (only reached after --wait expires with nothing new) |
| `--wait` | `20s` | hold each request open this long when caught up, so an event is reported as it lands rather than at the next --interval tick. The engine clamps its own ceiling; 0 = pure polling |

## `khora events list`

List lifecycle events

```text
khora events list [flags]
```

| Option | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--after` | `0` | sequence number to start after |
| `--limit` | `0` | maximum events to return |

## `khora files download`

Download a file from a running sandbox.

Pass - as the local path to write to stdout.

## `khora network`

Manage network configuration

```text
khora network
```

Aliases: `net`

## `khora network get`

Show a sandbox's network declaration.

The output is a legal input to 'network patch' — that is a contract requirement, not a
convenience: editing a declaration is a read-modify-write, and a patch built from a
stale read silently drops a publish added in between, on a security-relevant field.

Read it while PAUSED. Reading before the pause pulls the whole pause window into the
window where that lost update can happen.

```text
khora network get <sandbox-id>
```

## `khora network patch`

Replace a sandbox's network declaration, whole.

WHOLESALE IS THE CONTRACT: there is no field-level edit of a declaration, because merge
semantics on an allow-list is how a rule gets dropped without anyone deciding to drop
it. Whatever you pass here becomes the entire declaration.

The safe sequence is: pause, network get, edit, network patch, resume. Editing the
egress fields on a running sandbox is a conflict.

```text
khora network patch <sandbox-id> [flags]
```

| Option | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--json` | `""` | the complete network declaration as JSON (required) |

## `khora network publish`

Publish a guest port.

Legal on a running sandbox, unlike an egress edit — the record and the kernel rules are
one un-halvable write. On a paused sandbox it is recorded and takes effect at the next
placement, which the reported 'applies_at' distinguishes; both are a success.

```text
khora network publish <sandbox-id> [flags]
```

| Option | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--guest-port` | `0` | the guest port to publish (required) |
| `--proto` | `tcp` | tcp or udp |

## `khora sandbox`

Manage sandboxes

```text
khora sandbox
```

Aliases: `sb`

## `khora sandbox activity`

Record one activity on a running sandbox.

For work the engine cannot see: a long computation that does no I/O through the
engine's own paths still looks idle to it, and this says otherwise.

It carries NO DURATION. It records one activity now — it is not a lease, not a
keepalive, and not a pause-inhibit, because each of those would have the engine promise
to protect the sandbox for a period. To hold a sandbox open, call this on an interval
shorter than its idle timeout; the interval is yours.

A paused sandbox is a conflict, not a resume: the clock lives in the guest, so there is
nothing to stamp while frozen. An unreachable guest reports unavailable, for the same
reason — there is deliberately no host-side fallback, since a host timestamp would keep
a wedged sandbox alive forever.

```text
khora sandbox activity <sandbox-id>
```

| `--template` | `""` | template ID (required) |

## `khora sandbox delete`

Destroy a sandbox and its record.

IRREVERSIBLE, and the record goes with it: afterwards a get is a not-found and the
death cause is gone. If you need to know why a sandbox ended, read it before destroying,
or take it from the destroyed event's cause — there is no post-hoc query, because there
is no row left to query.

```text
khora sandbox delete <sandbox-id>
```

Aliases: `rm`

## `khora sandbox patch`

Rewrite parts of a sandbox's binding.

Only the flags you pass are sent, which is what makes "leave this axis alone"
distinguishable from "set it to 0" — and 0 is itself meaningful here (0 = unlimited for
a cap, retention 0 = never evict).

Resource caps are editable while paused; see the API contract for which axes a running
sandbox refuses.

```text
khora sandbox patch <sandbox-id> [flags]
```

| Option | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--cpu-millis` | `0` | CPU millicores cap (0 = unlimited) |
| `--disk-byte` | `0` | disk cap in bytes (0 = unlimited) |
| `--idle-timeout` | `""` | idle timeout duration (e.g. 30m) |
| `--memory-byte` | `0` | memory cap in bytes (0 = unlimited) |
| `--retention` | `""` | retention duration (0 = never evict) |

## `khora sandbox pause`

Pause a sandbox.

In-flight engine writes are drained first, then the sandbox is frozen. The reported
state is read back after the verb, so it is the achieved state rather than the requested
one.

```text
khora sandbox pause <sandbox-id>
```

## `khora sandbox resume`

Resume a paused sandbox.

The sandbox comes back on a FRESH placement, so its host endpoint and any published
port endpoints are new. Re-read them rather than reusing what you held before the
pause.

```text
khora sandbox resume <sandbox-id>
```

## `khora template delete`

Delete a template.

A template some sandbox was built from is refused as a conflict: its layers are still in
use underneath those sandboxes.

```text
khora template delete <template-id>
```

## `khora template promote`

Promote a sandbox's filesystem into a reusable template.

The template ID is minted by the engine and printed on success — it is not yours to
choose, because the engine's IDs are the only names it guarantees.

```text

```

| Option | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--from` | `""` | the sandbox to promote (required) |


| `--size` | `0` | clone size in bytes (0 = uncapped) |

## `khora volume create`

Create a volume.

A volume's lifetime is independent of any sandbox's — that is the point of the
subsystem. Attach it by naming it in a sandbox's volume binding at create time or on a
patch.

--size 0 means uncapped.

```text
khora volume create [flags]
```

| Option | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--idempotency-key` | `""` | retry key for durable create convergence |
| `--size` | `0` | volume size in bytes (0 = uncapped) |

## `khora volume delete`

Delete a volume.

A volume some sandbox still binds is refused as a conflict — detach it first by patching
that sandbox's volume binding.

```text
khora volume delete <volume-id>
```

Aliases: `rm`

## `khora volume export`

```text
khora volume export <volume-id> <remote-path> [local-path]
```

## `khora volume get`

Show one volume, including its usage

```text

```

## `khora volume import`

Write a file into a volume directly.

No running sandbox is needed: the host reaches the volume through a root-confined
accessor, so a volume can be seeded before anything mounts it. The remote path is
relative to the volume root, and a traversal clamps inside the volume rather than
erroring.

```text
khora volume import <volume-id> <local-path> <remote-path>
```

## `khora volume patch`

Resize a volume.

A cap that is not strictly greater than current usage is refused rather than applied —
shrinking below what is stored would make the quota unenforceable rather than free any
space. Run 'volume get' first if you need to know the floor.

```text
khora volume patch <volume-id> [flags]
```

| Option | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--size` | `0` | new volume size in bytes (required) |
